{"id": "14:36/q03", "question": "How can idols be said to lead people astray?", "turns_on": "Whether misguidance is purely figurative causation or is also mediated by devils inhabiting idols.", "positions": [{"id": "14:36/q03/p1", "position": "The attribution is figurative or causal: people stray by worshipping or attaching themselves to lifeless idols.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba offers both 'caused to stray' and 'strayed through them.' Kashshaf, Nasafi, Abu Hayyan, Baydawi, Bursevi, and others compare worldly life deluding people (6:70). Razi says all theological schools agree the attribution is metaphorical; Ibn Atiyya and Alusi add that God actually creates misguidance. {"id": "14:36/q05", "question": "What does following Abraham and being 'of him' mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the affiliation is described as Abraham's religious community or as an inward relation to the spirit.", "positions": [{"id": "14:36/q05/p1", "position": "Following his monotheistic religion, teaching, and way makes one a member of his religious community, closely attached to him.", "reasons": "Tabari specifies worship of God alone and abandonment of idols; Ibn Abbas adds knowledge of God. Ibn al-Anbari cites a poem where not being 'of' someone means not adhering to his covenant. Kashshaf, Baydawi, Nasafi, Abu Hayyan, and Bursevi stress closeness like an inseparable part; Kashshaf and Abu Hayyan compare the saying that a cheat is not 'of us,' a grave departure from believers' traits. Al-Samin glosses 'of me' as follower or party. Al-Biqa'i connects this to avoiding idols and hoped-for success. Tabataba'i insists on the whole path of belief and practice, rather than bare affirmation of oneness; the path image answers the preceding straying. Al-Alusi includes the call to monotheism and Islam. Kur'an Yolu includes salvation for protected believers. Razi treats religious belief as making a follower almost a part of Abraham, while disobedience outside religion remains subject to mercy. Bursevi calls min partitive; Alusi allows partitive simile or connective affiliation; al-Sharif and al-Suyuti explain the specific implied relation."}, {"id": "14:36/q05/p2", "position": "Inwardly, following the spirit on the path of tawhid makes one belong to it.", "reasons": "Qashani describes spiritual affiliation through following the spirit."}]}
{"id": "14:36/q06", "question": "Who counts as Abraham's descendants or true heirs in this prayer?", "turns_on": "The scope of spiritual kinship beyond biological descent.", "positions": [{"id": "14:36/q06/p1", "position": "Spiritual allegiance admits later followers and can exclude disobedient biological descendants.", "reasons": "Tabataba'i says this interprets 'my sons'; like 2:126 it broadens blessing to followers and limits protected descendants. He invokes 3:68 for the Prophet and believers, and Noah's son excluded from his family in 11:46. He reports two nuances: Abraham may disown all disobedient people, or merely be silent about their affiliation. His earlier discussion takes that silence as disowning and as evidence for a faithful line. Razi also uses Noah's son to confine the prayer to believing descendants. Asad notes Abraham accepts God's verdict on sinful descendants in 2:124."}, {"id": "14:36/q06/p2", "position": "Abraham's words also support including devoted followers of the Imams among the Prophet's family.", "reasons": "In two al-Ayyashi reports, al-Sadiq applies 'of me' to lovers of the Imams, and to those who fear God and act righteously; he and Umar ibn Yazid also cite 3:68."}]}

{"id": "14:36/q17", "question": "Who established the order of the suras in which this prayer appears?", "turns_on": "Whether sura order came by explicit revelation or Prophetic instruction, an implied pattern allowing judgment, or Companion arrangement.", "positions": [{"id": "14:36/q17/p1", "position": "The order was divinely or prophetically fixed before codex collection.", "reasons": "Al-Kirmani places it in the Preserved Tablet and Gabriel's annual reviews, twice in the last year; al-Tibi adds descent to the lowest heaven and later compilation in that order. {"id": "14:36/q19", "question": "Why did Abraham ask protection against idol worship even for himself?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "14:36/q19/p1", "position": "His inclusion of himself underscores the grave danger of polytheism, since idols had drawn many astray.", "reasons": "Islahi stresses the breadth of that danger despite Abraham's standing."}]}

{"id": "14:37/q01", "question": "Why is Abraham's invocation repeated and phrased as 'Our Lord'?", "turns_on": "Whether the plural points to these descendants or to earlier sons, and how the intervening address functions.", "positions": [{"id": "14:37/q01/p1", "position": "It renews humble supplication and draws attention to the request.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān says repetition seeks an answer; Ibn ʿĀshūr calls it a new prayer; Bursevī and Iṣlāḥī stress repeated humble appeal."}, {"id": "14:37/q01/p2", "position": "The plural includes the family for whom Abraham prays.", "reasons": "Bursevī and Ibn ʿĀshūr include the sons; Ālūsī prefers the descendants in this request over al-Baḥr's link to sons in 14:35, since 14:36 then lacks a plural."}, {"id": "14:37/q01/p3", "position": "The repeated address emphasizes prayer as the settlement's purpose.", "reasons": "Bayḍāwī and Ālūsī highlight prayer; al-Kashf infers an omitted verb after the vocative, which Ālūsī rejects."}, {"id": "14:37/q01/p4", "position": "The plural follows the sons mentioned earlier.", "reasons": "Al-Baḥr links it to 14:35; Ālūsī objects by comparison with 14:36."}, {"id": "14:37/q01/p5", "position": "Rabbi invokes a personally experienced favor; Rabbana a favor witnessed by all.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī distinguishes these forms of address."}]}

{"id": "14:37/q10", "question": "What does 'without cultivation' imply about the valley?", "turns_on": "Whether infertility implies lack of water or deliberately leaves future water open.", "positions": [{"id": "14:37/q10/p1", "position": "It emphatically excludes cultivation and describes land unfit for crops.", "reasons": "Zamakhsharī, Rāzī, Bursevī, Ālūsī, Ibn ʿĀshūr and Ṭabāṭabāʾī compare 39:28. {"id": "14:37/q11", "question": "What is meant by 'Your Sacred House' and why is it attributed to God?", "turns_on": "The literal sanctuary and an inward symbol.", "positions": [{"id": "14:37/q11/p1", "position": "The Kaaba or sanctuary, belonging to or honored by God.", "reasons": "Māwardī calls it the qibla; Ṭabrisī, Qurtubī and Jishumī say God alone owns it, Abū ʿAlī says the attribution commands honor, and Ṭabāṭabāʾī links ownership to exclusive worship."}, {"id": "14:37/q11/p2", "position": "Inwardly, the heart reserved for God.", "reasons": "Qāshānī and al-Taʾwīlāt al-Najmiyya give the symbol."}]}

{"id": "14:37/q13", "question": "Why is the House called 'al-muharram'?", "turns_on": "The prohibition, protective status, honor, Flood history or primordial sanctity named by the adjective.", "positions": [{"id": "14:37/q13/p1", "position": "God prohibited violating it and made its precinct sacred.", "reasons": "Qatāda forbids disrespect; others mention fighting, hunting, blood and filth. ʿUmar says Ṭasm and Jurhum perished for violation; Ibn ʿĀshūr cites aggressors and the Elephant."}, {"id": "14:37/q13/p2", "position": "It has always been protected and feared by tyrants.", "reasons": "Zamakhsharī, Rāzī, Nasafī and others describe its impregnable status; Jishumī adds no tyrant owns it."}, {"id": "14:37/q13/p3", "position": "The Flood did not overtake it.", "reasons": "Zamakhsharī, Rāzī, Bayḍāwī and others compare al-ʿAtīq, freed from the Flood."}, {"id": "14:37/q13/p4", "position": "Visitors must enter consecration and abstain from otherwise lawful acts.", "reasons": "Māwardī mentions sex; Jishumī and Ṭabrisī mention impurity and iḥrām; Ālūsī rejects this derivation."}, {"id": "14:37/q13/p5", "position": "It is greatly honored and revered.", "reasons": "Zamakhsharī, Rāzī, Nasafī and Ṭabrisī give this sense."}, {"id": "14:37/q13/p6", "position": "Its sacred status dates to creation.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās says seven angels surrounded it; Ibn al-Sāʾib dates sanctification to creation; Rāzī mentions Adam's heavenly counterpart."}]}
{"id": "14:37/q14", "question": "How do the location phrases attach syntactically?", "turns_on": "Whether the House phrase modifies settling or the valley.", "positions": [{"id": "14:37/q14/p1", "position": "The valley phrase locates settlement, and 'at Your House' modifies 'I settled'.", "reasons": "Akhfash and al-Samīn gloss bi-wādin as 'in a valley'; Bursevī, Ālūsī and Ṭabāṭabāʾī make the House phrase adverbial."}, {"id": "14:37/q14/p2", "position": "'At Your House' describes or apposes 'valley'.", "reasons": "Abū al-Baqāʾ suggests adjective or partitive apposition; al-Samīn objects that ʿinda is noninflecting, and Ālūsī prefers adverbial attachment; Ibn ʿĀshūr allows a second adjective or circumstantial phrase."}]}

{"id": "14:37/q30", "question": "Why did Abraham ask that hearts incline toward them?", "turns_on": "Sustaining the family and developing pilgrimage.", "positions": [{"id": "14:37/q30/p1", "position": "Visitors would comfort the family, sustain them and enable worship.", "reasons": "Jishumī, Ṭabrisī, Rāzī and Asad say pilgrimage and trade bring food, clothing and company. Qushayrī stresses freedom for worship; Ibn ʿĀshūr says affection builds town familiarity, markets and rites."}, {"id": "14:37/q30/p2", "position": "The attraction establishes a pilgrimage center.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan says God made Hajj obligatory; Iṣlāḥī says the House attracted Arabia and later the world."}]}
{"id": "14:37/q31", "question": "How is a similar prayer applied to Medina?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "14:37/q31/p1", "position": "The Prophet prayed for Medina's measures to be blessed and hearts to incline toward its people.", "reasons": "Abū Hurayra reports the parallel Prophetic prayer."}]}
{"id": "14:37/q32", "question": "What fruits were requested?", "turns_on": "Material produce versus inward fruit.", "positions": [{"id": "14:37/q32/p1", "position": "Literal fruits and produce brought to an uncultivated valley.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī compares watered regions; Māwardī names palms and trees; Rāzī says a portion; Bayḍāwī says many kinds were supplied."}, {"id": "14:37/q32/p2", "position": "Fruits of the heart: belovedness attracting visitors.", "reasons": "Māwardī reports this inward explanation."}, {"id": "14:37/q32/p3", "position": "Universal knowledge and realities.", "reasons": "Qāshānī pairs this inward fruit with perfection through grateful perception."}]}
{"id": "14:37/q33", "question": "How were fruits supplied to Mecca?", "turns_on": "Transport and cultivation versus miraculous relocation reports.", "positions": [{"id": "14:37/q33/p1", "position": "Imports through pilgrimage and trade, including nearby Taif and distant lands.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī, Zamakhsharī, Jishumī and Abū Ḥayyān connect this with 28:57; some mention nearby cultivation and several seasons' fruits at once. {"id": "14:37/q34", "question": "Who receives the provision?", "turns_on": "Whether later residents share the request.", "positions": [{"id": "14:37/q34/p1", "position": "The settled descendants, perhaps also those who join them.", "reasons": "Bursevī and Ālūsī include both, contrasting 2:126; Qurtubī says it sustains Mecca's people."}, {"id": "14:37/q34/p2", "position": "Hagar and Ishmael specifically.", "reasons": "Study Quran states this form of the request."}]}
{"id": "14:37/q35", "question": "What does 'so that they may give thanks' entail?", "turns_on": "Material gratitude and worship versus inward use of knowledge.", "positions": [{"id": "14:37/q35/p1", "position": "Thank God for provision through worship, prayer and acknowledgment of His oneness.", "reasons": "Māwardī glosses 'thank You'; Wāḥidī says affirm oneness and exalt Him; Bursevī and Ālūsī specify rites. {"id": "14:37/q36", "question": "Why does security precede these requests in Abraham's prayer?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "14:37/q36/p1", "position": "Security is the greatest blessing and makes religious and worldly life possible.", "reasons": "Rāzī reads the request order this way; a scholar compares a sheep that can recover from injury with one too afraid of a wolf to graze."}]}
{"id": "14:37/q37", "question": "What does the verse teach about reliance and worship?", "turns_on": "The degree of reliance and its relation to material means.", "positions": [{"id": "14:37/q37/p1", "position": "Abraham entrusted his family to God so they could worship despite deprivation.", "reasons": "Qushayrī stresses reliance over comforts; Jishumī says God turned hearts to sustain them; Rāzī makes provision serve obligations. Iṣlāḥī says worship can require sacrifice; Qurtubī limits the story to Abraham's divine command."}, {"id": "14:37/q37/p2", "position": "The barren valley symbolizes leaving created supports for God.", "reasons": "Sulamī's Ibn ʿAṭāʾ and others describe freedom from convention and material causes; Qushayrī says inner selves attach to no worldly other."}, {"id": "14:37/q37/p3", "position": "The family is honored insofar as God cares for them.", "reasons": "Qushayrī says their honor and weakness depend on God's decree."}]}
{"id": "14:37/q38", "question": "How does the prayer connect with other verses and the sūrah?", "turns_on": "Parallel prayers and the sūrah's contrast of gratitude with ingratitude.", "positions": [{"id": "14:37/q38/p1", "position": "It parallels 2:126 and God's answer in 28:57.", "reasons": "Wāḥidī cites the parallel request; Burhān contrasts baladan and al-balad syntax; Ibn ʿĀshūr says the city is unnamed for suspense or familiarity. {"id": "14:37/q39", "question": "What analogies about Arabic forms appear with the verse's grammatical notes?", "turns_on": "Different general form rules cited in associated notes.", "positions": [{"id": "14:37/q39/p1", "position": "Deleted radicals can reappear in nisba forms.", "reasons": "Sībawayh gives dam, yad, ghad, thab, shaf and ḥar, with poetry and plurals; doubled forms avoid an awkward geminate."}, {"id": "14:37/q39/p2", "position": "A stopped hāʾ can transfer its vowel to a preceding consonant.", "reasons": "Sībawayh gives poetry and Banū ʿAdī's kasra examples, which do not mark case."}, {"id": "14:37/q39/p3", "position": "Nominal patterns differ in declension and diptosis by alteration, definiteness and diminutive.", "reasons": "Sībawayh surveys ḥuṭam, distributives, ʿUmar, Zufar, Zuhal, Jamʿ, Kutaʿ, Akhar, Qāl/Qīl and reduced names, citing 35:1 and poetry."}, {"id": "14:37/q39/p4", "position": "A quiescent wāw after kasra may become yāʾ, with morphological exceptions.", "reasons": "Sībawayh contrasts mīzān/miʿād with mawʿid/mawqif and discusses vocalized wāw, nouns, verbs, masdars and feminine compensation."}, {"id": "14:37/q39/p5", "position": "A disputed temporal particle usage lacks attestation in Arabic.", "reasons": "Al-Ṣaffār says Arabic uses madh or mundhu instead."}]}
